Venerable

/VEN-ur-uh-bul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Venerable means deserving deep respect because of age, wisdom, or great achievement.

The venerable dictionary, in print since 1857, still settles arguments no app can.

Worked Example

Every town meeting in Alcott's Green happens under the same elm — the one planted the year the town was chartered, the one settlers' letters mention by name, the one the road crew rerouted an entire lane to spare. Nobody voted to make the tree venerable; two centuries of shade, history, and stubborn survival did that on their own.

The tree's two centuries of history and the town's instinct to protect and gather beneath it show respect earned by age and endurance — the essence of venerable.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

respected: held in high regard

esteemed: greatly valued and honored

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unproven: not yet having demonstrated worth

newfangled: new and untested, often distrusted

Where it sits · how close to sacred the esteem grows — respected → venerable → hallowed

respected vs. venerable: Respected people are valued; a venerable person or institution has accumulated so much age, wisdom, or achievement that the respect deepens into something close to awe.

hallowed vs. venerable: Hallowed goes beyond venerable — the respect has turned fully sacred, as for holy ground.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vener

Root — vener: to regard with awe, to worship (Latin venerari)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: worthy of; able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Venerable joins Latin venerari, 'to regard with awe or worship,' to the suffix -able, 'worthy of.' A venerable person or institution is literally 'worthy of veneration' — and unlike most -able words, this one is almost always earned the slow way, through decades or centuries of wisdom, service, and survival.

Use the root in a new word: veneration

Use the root in a new word: veneration: Pilgrims gazed at the ancient shrine with open veneration — the noun from the same Latin root venerari, 'to regard with awe,' that makes an institution venerable.

Word Choice

formal, dignified; for people and institutions alike

Venerable names a quality someone or something has — respect earned through age, wisdom, or achievement — while revere (also in this unit) names what admirers do in response; reputable, the unit's third respect word, is far cooler and more transactional, meaning simply trustworthy and not shady, with no awe, age, or grandeur required.
